paras.text: Carpentry and Structural Framing, Audio Lecture
This is the single biggest trade category on your exam. Sixteen of the one hundred ten trade questions come from carpentry and framing, and nothing else comes close.

Almost every one of them is a number. A fraction of a joist depth. A percentage of a stud width. A nail count. An inch measurement. Numbers can be drilled, so that is what we are going to do, walking the house from the floor up to the roof, then out to the stairs and the deck.

One thing before we start, and it shapes the whole chapter. The exam tests the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code. Not the twenty twenty one I R C. The newer code was stayed by a court order in July of twenty twenty five and never took effect.

That matters because Michigan amended some values away from the national defaults, and the exam builds its wrong answers out of the national number. Every time I flag a Michigan amendment, that is your cue to burn it in twice, because the wrong answer will be the one you have read in every national book.
Idea one. Where joists land, and where they need help.
Every joist, beam, or girder needs bearing at its ends. One and a half inches minimum on wood or metal. Three inches minimum on masonry or concrete.
One and a half on wood, three on concrete. Say it back.

And a detail with a reason attached. If a wood girder pockets into a concrete or block wall, it gets that three inches of bearing plus a half inch air space around the untreated wood, so it can dry instead of rot.

Joist ends also need lateral restraint, meaning something that keeps them from rolling over. Full depth solid blocking of at least two inch nominal, or attachment to a full depth header, band joist, rim joist, or an adjoining stud.

Now mid span, and here is a Michigan exam classic. Bridging, which means solid blocking, diagonal bridging, or a one by three strip nailed across the bottoms, is only required for joists that exceed a nominal two by twelve. When it is required, the intervals cannot exceed eight feet.

Hear the trap inside that. A two by ten does not need bridging. A two by twelve does not need bridging. Only joists deeper than a two by twelve. And the wrong answer on your exam will say two by ten, because that is what a lot of people were taught in the field.
Idea two. Cutting, drilling, and notching, which is one pattern of fractions.
This shows up constantly, so learn it as a pattern rather than four separate rules.

Notches in the top or bottom of a joist. Maximum depth one sixth of the joist depth. The notch cannot be longer than one third of the depth. And no notches at all in the middle third of the span, because that is where the bending is worst.
At the very end of the joist, over a bearing, the notch can be deeper, up to one fourth of the depth.
Holes have their own rule. Maximum diameter one third of the depth, and every hole stays at least two inches away from the top edge, the bottom edge, any other hole, and any notch.
So the pattern is, one sixth for notches in the span, one fourth for notches at the ends, one third for holes and for notch length, and two inches of clearance from everything.

Run it on a real board. A two by ten is actually nine and a quarter inches deep. So a notch is about an inch and a half. An end notch is about two and five sixteenths. A hole is about three and one sixteenth.

Now the exception that is worth an easy point. Engineered lumber is a different world. You do not cut, notch, or drill an I joist, an L V L, a glulam, or a truss. Not at all, unless the manufacturer's literature allows it or an engineer signs off.
Those pre stamped knockouts in an I joist web are the manufacturer's permission, which is why they exist. And a truss that got field cut needs a registered design professional to fix it.
Question. Two by ten joist, nine and a quarter inches deep. How deep can you notch it mid span, and where can you not notch it at all.
One sixth of the depth, so about an inch and a half. And never in the middle third of the span.
Idea three. Floor openings and cantilevers.
For an opening like a stairwell, the rule steps up twice.
If the header joist span is four feet or less, a single header the same size as the joists is fine, with single trimmers, as long as the header lands within three feet of the trimmer bearing.
Once the header span goes over four feet, you double the header and double the trimmers.
Over six feet, you hang it on approved joist hangers.
Four feet, double. Six feet, hangers. Two steps, two numbers.
And if you have double joists under a parallel bearing partition that get spread apart for piping, you block between them, full depth, two inch nominal lumber, at no more than four feet on center.

Cantilevers, and here is another twenty twenty one trap. The twenty fifteen code says a prescriptive floor cantilever cannot exceed the nominal depth of the joist. So a two by ten hangs out about ten inches. Beyond that you are into the cantilever tables.

You may have heard the L over four rule, cantilever equals a quarter of the back span. That is a deck rule out of the twenty twenty one I R C, and it is not in the tested code. If the question says per the code, the answer is the depth rule and the tables.
Idea four. Walls, studs, and the four percentages.
Stud sizes first, and it works as a ladder of what is stacked on top.
A two by four bearing wall carrying just a roof and ceiling can go twenty four inches on center, up to ten feet tall.
Add one floor above and those two by fours drop to sixteen inches on center.
Two floors plus a roof, and two by fours are out entirely. You need two by sixes at sixteen.

Nonbearing two by fours can run twenty four on center up to fourteen feet. And utility grade studs are the cheap seats, sixteen on center maximum, roof and ceiling only, eight feet maximum in exterior walls.
Top plates are doubled, overlapped at corners and intersections, with end joints offset at least twenty four inches.

There is a single top plate exception, and it comes with its own hardware. A three by six inch, twenty gauge galvanized splice plate with six eight penny nails on each side. Hold onto twenty gauge, because a different plate is coming in a minute and the exam puts them side by side.
Now the four percentages for studs, and this is the wire they want you to cross.
Notching. Twenty five percent of the stud width in a bearing or exterior wall. Forty percent in a nonbearing partition.
Boring. Forty percent in a single bearing stud. Sixty percent in a nonbearing stud, or in a bearing stud if you double the studs, and you can only bore two successive doubled studs that way.
Every bored hole stays five eighths of an inch from the edge of the stud, and never in the same cross section as a notch.
So notch is twenty five and forty. Bore is forty and sixty. Notice that forty percent appears on both lists, notching a nonbearing stud and boring a bearing stud. That overlap is the trap.

And the top plate repair, the one with the other gauge. When somebody cuts or notches more than fifty percent of a bearing wall top plate, usually the plumber running a vent, the fix is a galvanized metal tie, sixteen gauge, an inch and a half wide, nailed with eight ten penny nails on each side, extending at least six inches past the opening.
Sixteen gauge repair tie. Twenty gauge single plate splice. Two plates, two gauges, two jobs.
Question. Bearing wall stud. What is the maximum notch, and what is the maximum bored hole.
Notch twenty five percent of the stud width. Bore forty percent, or sixty percent if you double the studs.
Idea five. Headers and wall bracing.
Headers over doors and windows come out of the header tables, sized by the header's lumber, the snow load, and the building width. The same table tells you how many jack studs go under each end.
Jack studs, also called trimmers, are cut to header height and carry the load. King studs run full height beside them. Jack carries, king ties it together.

Wall bracing. Every exterior wall line is a braced wall line. Along it, a braced wall panel has to begin within ten feet of each end of the line, with no more than twenty feet between adjacent panels. Ten from the ends, twenty between.

Know the method letters, because they will use the abbreviations. L I B is a one by four let in brace. W S P is wood structural panel, minimum three eighths inch. G B is gypsum board. C S dash W S P is continuous sheathing.

And remember what governs here. In Michigan, wind governs bracing, not earthquakes, because we are seismic design category A or B. That is the same reason the anchor bolt seismic spacing did not apply back in the foundation chapter.
Idea six. The roof, and the tie question that is almost guaranteed.

Start with the ridge. The ridge board is at least one inch nominal thick, and at least as deep as the cut end of the rafter. Valley and hip rafters are beefier, two inch nominal minimum, same depth rule.

And when the roof pitch drops below three in twelve, a ridge board is not enough. The ridge, hips, and valleys have to be designed as beams. Low slope means the geometry stops helping you, so the member has to carry it.
Now the tie question. Rafter ties versus collar ties. If you learn one thing from this section, learn this.

Rafter ties, usually your ceiling joists, sit down low at the plate. Their job is to resist the outward thrust that wants to push your walls apart. Minimum two by four when installed as dedicated ties.
Collar ties sit up high, in the upper third of the attic, minimum one by four, no more than four feet on center. Their job is to resist wind uplift at the ridge.
Low ties stop spreading. High ties stop uplift. Say that one twice, because the words sound alike and the jobs are opposite.
And the consequence. If your ceiling joists run perpendicular to the rafters, or are not connected at the plate, you add rafter ties or you engineer a ridge beam. Something has to take that thrust.
A few more roof numbers. Ceiling joists lap at least three inches over bearing partitions, or butt and get toenailed.

Purlins, which shorten rafter spans, must be at least the size of the rafters they support, braced down to bearing walls with two by fours at forty five degrees or steeper, braces four feet on center maximum, and no brace longer than eight feet unbraced.
And rafter notching follows the exact same fractions as joists. One sixth, one fourth at the ends, one third for holes. Same pattern, second time you have heard it.
Question. Which tie stops the walls from spreading, where does it sit, and what is the minimum size.
The rafter tie. Down low at the plate, minimum two by four. Collar ties are the high ones in the upper third, minimum one by four, and they handle uplift.
Idea seven. The fastening schedule, table R six oh two point three.
Nobody memorizes the whole table. Learn the greatest hits, because that is what gets asked.
Joist to sill or girder, three eight penny toenails. Ceiling joist to plate, the same, three eight penny toenails.
Top plate to top plate, sixteen penny commons at sixteen inches on center. Double top plate splice, eight sixteen penny nails on each side of the joint.
Stud to plate, two sixteen penny end nails. Collar tie to rafter, three ten penny face nails. Band joist to joist, three sixteen penny end nails.
Built up girders, twenty penny nails at thirty two inches on center top and bottom, staggered, with two more at every end and splice.
And structural sheathing, six inches on center at the panel edges, twelve in the field. Six and twelve. Edges get twice the nails because that is where panels move.
Idea eight. Stairs, which is Michigan's signature amendment.
Lock this down, because it is one of the most likely questions on your whole exam.
Minimum tread depth, nine inches. Maximum riser height, eight and a quarter inches.
The I R C says ten inch treads and seven and three quarter risers. In Michigan those are the trap answers.

And notice the direction of each rule, because it explains something that confuses people. Nine is a minimum and eight and a quarter is a maximum. So a stair built to the stricter national numbers still passes here. Michigan is more permissive, not less.

Risers and treads cannot vary more than three eighths of an inch within a flight. That small number is a real safety rule, because your foot learns the first step and expects every other one to match.
Winders. Ten inches of tread at the walk line, which is twelve inches from the narrow side, and six inches minimum anywhere.
Headroom, six feet eight inches.
Width, thirty six inches clear. Thirty one and a half with one handrail. Twenty seven with two.
Handrails kick in at four or more risers, set thirty four to thirty eight inches above the nosings, and a round rail grips at an inch and a quarter to two inches.
Guards are required when the walking surface is more than thirty inches up. At least thirty six inches high, no opening that passes a four inch sphere, and built to take a two hundred pound load.
Thirty triggers the guard, thirty six is its height, four inch sphere, two hundred pounds.
Question. Michigan stairs. Minimum tread, maximum riser, and what triggers a guard.
Nine inch tread minimum, eight and a quarter inch riser maximum. Ten and seven and three quarters are the national trap. And a guard is required over thirty inches of drop, at thirty six inches high.
Idea nine. Decks.

The ledger is where decks kill people, so the code is specific. Minimum two by eight, pressure treated, number two grade. Bolted or lag screwed with half inch hot dipped galvanized or stainless fasteners.
Never electroplated. The treated lumber chemistry eats them.
Spacing comes off the table based on joist span, staggered in two rows, and it gets flashed where it meets the house.
Where hold downs provide the lateral connection, it is two devices minimum, fifteen hundred pounds each.
Deck footings go to Michigan frost depth. Forty two inches, same as the house, and you already own that number from the foundation chapter.
And one last twenty twenty one trap. The deck post height table, four by four up to eight feet, six by six up to fourteen feet, is not in the tested code. That is the twenty twenty one I R C again.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me.

Bearing, one and a half on wood, three on masonry. Bridging, only past a two by twelve, at eight foot intervals. Joist notch one sixth, end notch one fourth, hole one third, two inch clearances, no notches in the middle third. Opening headers, double past four feet, hangers past six. Stud notch twenty five bearing, forty nonbearing. Stud bore forty bearing, sixty nonbearing or doubled. Five eighths edge distance. Plate cut past fifty percent, sixteen gauge tie, inch and a half wide, eight ten penny each side, six inches past the cut. Plate joints offset twenty four. Two by four studs, twenty four on center roof only, sixteen with a floor above, two by six for two floors. Ridge board one inch, hips and valleys two inch, designed as beams below three in twelve. Collar ties upper third, one by four, four feet. Ceiling joist lap three inches. Purlin braces two by four, forty five degrees, four feet on center, eight feet maximum. Top plates sixteen penny at sixteen. Sheathing six and twelve. Stairs, nine inch tread, eight and a quarter riser, three eighths variation, six eight headroom, thirty six wide, handrail at four risers, thirty four to thirty eight. Guards, thirty inches triggers, thirty six high, four inch sphere, two hundred pounds. Deck, two by eight treated ledger, half inch galvanized bolts, fifteen hundred pound hold downs, forty two inch footings.

Sixteen questions live in those numbers. The three I would drill first are the nine and eight and a quarter stairs, because that is Michigan's own amendment, the stud percentages, because of the forty percent overlap, and rafter ties versus collar ties, because the words are so easy to swap. Run it again tomorrow and they are yours.
